5940: To "fall between two stools" means to fail because you tried to be two things at once, or aim for two goals at once, and ended up achieving neither.

Before understanding the idiom, picture this:

Imagine two wooden stools placed a little apart from each other. Someone tries to sit on both stools at the same time — one foot on one stool, the other foot on the other. What happens? They lose their balance and fall into the gap between the two stools.

That physical image — falling into the empty space between two things — is exactly what this idiom describes, but in a non-physical, everyday-life sense.
What It Really Means (The Two Closely Related Senses)

This idiom is used in two closely connected ways. Both come from the same core idea.

Sense 1: Trying to Do Two Things and Failing at Both

When someone tries to achieve two different goals at the same time, but because they are pulled in two directions, they end up doing neither well — they "fall between two stools."

The key idea here is that the attempt to do both is what causes the failure. If they had focused on just one, they might have succeeded. But by splitting their attention and effort, they fell into the gap.

Examples:

  • A writer tries to make her novel both a serious, deep literary masterpiece and a light, fun beach read. She tries so hard to be both that the book ends up being neither truly deep nor truly fun. Her novel falls between two stools.
  • A restaurant tries to be both a cheap fast-food joint and a fancy fine-dining experience. The food isn't cheap enough for budget customers, and it isn't elegant enough for fine-dining customers. It falls between two stools and loses both types of customers.
  • A student preparing for two exams on the same day splits his time equally between both. He doesn't study enough for either one and fails both. His preparation fell between two stools.

Sense 2: Not Fitting Into Either of Two Categories

This sense is slightly different. Here, something (or someone) ends up in an awkward middle ground — it doesn't clearly belong to one group or the other. It is too much of one thing to be the second, and too much of the second thing to be the first. So it sits uncomfortably between both and fits into neither.

The "failure" here is not always the person's fault — sometimes it's just an awkward situation of being in-between.

Examples:

  • A book is too long and complex to be a children's book, but too simple and short to be a proper adult novel. It falls between two stools — publishers don't know which shelf to put it on.
  • A person applies for a job. They have some experience — more than a complete beginner, but far less than a senior professional. They are too experienced for the entry-level job but too inexperienced for the senior job. They fall between two stools and get neither.
  • A new movie tries to be both a documentary and a fictional drama. It ends up being not realistic enough for documentary fans and not entertaining enough for drama fans. It falls between two stools.

How Sense 1 and Sense 2 Connect

Both senses share the same soul: there are two clear positions/goals, you are caught in the middle, and you end up with nothing. In Sense 1, you actively tried to be both. In Sense 2, you ended up in between without necessarily intending to. In real usage, the two senses often blur together.

This idiom is very old — it goes back to at least the 14th century, making it one of the older idioms in the English language.

The earliest known written record in English is from the poet John Gower, who in 1390 wrote something that translates roughly to: "Between two stools my drunk man falls." Similar expressions existed in Latin and French even earlier, which tells us this was a common idea across cultures in medieval Europe.

In those times, stools (simple seats with no back) were the most common form of seating. People sitting down to eat or rest would use stools constantly. The image of someone clumsily trying to sit on two stools and falling would have been instantly funny and relatable to everyone who heard it — much like how we today might say someone "dropped the ball."

The idiom has survived for over 600 years and is still widely used today in British English in particular, though it is understood across all English-speaking regions.
How to Use It in a Sentence (Grammar Notes)

The idiom is a verb phrase. The verb "fall" changes depending on tense and subject, just like any regular verb. The rest of the phrase — "between two stools" — stays the same.

TenseExample
  • Present: "The project falls between two stools — it's not academic enough for researchers and not practical enough for businesses."
  • Past: "The campaign fell between two stools and failed to attract any clear audience."
  • Future: "If you try to please both groups, the plan will fall between two stools."
  • Present Perfect: "Their strategy has fallen between two stools once again."
  • Continuous/Participle: "The policy is in danger of falling between two stools if it isn't focused soon."

You can also use it about people, things, plans, projects, policies, books, films, or basically anything that can fail by being caught between two goals or categories.
The Tone and Register — When Is It Used?

This idiom is:

  • Neutral to slightly formal — it doesn't sound rude or very casual. It is perfectly fine in professional writing, academic essays, journalism, business meetings, and everyday conversation.
  • Mostly British in origin and frequency, but widely understood globally.
  • Often used when giving criticism or analysis — pointing out why something failed or is likely to fail.
  • Useful when you want to express a nuanced idea elegantly in just a few words. Instead of saying "They tried to do two things at once and ended up doing neither well," you simply say "It fell between two stools."
Similar Idioms — and How They Differ

Understanding related idioms helps you sharpen your understanding of this one.

1. "Jack of all trades, master of none"
This means someone who can do many things but is not excellent at any of them. The focus is on having too many skills spread thin, not just two. "Fall between two stools" is specifically about two things and often refers to a project or plan, not just a person's skills.

2. "Sit on the fence"
This means refusing to take a clear side or make a decision — being deliberately neutral. It's about indecision or cowardice. "Fall between two stools" is different — the person or thing does make an attempt, they just can't commit fully to either side and therefore fail. One is about avoiding a choice; the other is about failing despite (or because of) attempting both.

3. "Between a rock and a hard place"
This means being stuck between two bad or difficult options with no good way out. The focus is on difficulty and being trapped. "Fall between two stools" is about failing by not committing to either of two options — the options aren't necessarily bad, but the in-between position is.

4. "Two birds, one stone"
This is almost the opposite in spirit — it means achieving two goals with one action, successfully. "Fall between two stools" is what happens when the attempt to hit two birds at once goes wrong.
The Single Most Important Thing to Remember

If you want to lock the meaning into your memory forever, remember this one sentence:

You aimed for two things. You got neither. You fell between the two stools.

That's it. Any time something (a plan, a product, a person's effort, a piece of writing, a strategy) tries to serve two masters and ends up serving none — that thing has fallen between two stools.
Quick Real-World Scenarios to Test Your Understanding

Read each situation and confirm to yourself that you can see why the idiom applies:

  1. A politician tries to appeal to both very conservative voters and very liberal voters by taking no strong stance on anything. Neither group is impressed. → He fell between two stools.
  2. A new phone is designed to be both a luxury premium device and an affordable budget phone. It ends up too expensive for budget buyers and not premium enough for luxury buyers. → It falls between two stools.
  3. A chef tries to cook a dish that is both completely authentic Thai food and also suited to Western tastes, making it neither truly Thai nor truly Western. → The dish falls between two stools.

You now know everything there is to know about this idiom — its meaning in both senses, where it comes from, how old it is, how to use it grammatically, when to use it, how it differs from similar expressions, and how to spot it in real life. You're fully equipped.
5941:
When something or someone falls by the wayside, it means they fail to continue, get abandoned, or don't survive long enough to reach the finish line.

Think of a race with 50 runners. Not everyone finishes. Some get tired, some get injured, some simply stop. Those who drop out before the end — they "fell by the wayside." The ones who made it to the finish line did not.

The idiom captures the idea of something that started but didn't last.

This idiom is ancient. It comes from a famous story in the Bible called the Parable of the Sower (found in Matthew, Mark, and Luke in the New Testament).

In that story, a farmer scatters seeds across his land. Some seeds fall "by the wayside" — meaning on the hard, trampled ground along the edge of a path or road. Because the ground there is too hard for roots to grow, those seeds never sprout. Birds come and eat them. They are wasted — they had potential, but they came to nothing.

The word "wayside" simply means the side of a road or path. It's an old English word (wayside = way + side). In those times, roads were not perfectly defined, and the edges of paths were hard, barren ground — not the kind of soil where things grow.

So the literal image is: a seed that falls in a bad spot and never grows. Over time, this became a metaphor for anything that starts with promise but doesn't survive or succeed.

Today, people use this idiom in a few closely related ways:

1. A plan or goal gets abandoned.
You start something, but life gets in the way, and you stop. The thing is quietly dropped, forgotten, or never finished.

"She planned to learn the guitar, but that idea fell by the wayside after she started her new job."

2. A person doesn't make it through a process.
In competitions, job applications, training programs — many people start, but only some survive each stage. Those who get eliminated fall by the wayside.

"Out of 200 applicants, most fell by the wayside during the interview process."

3. Something loses priority and slowly disappears.
This is very common. You don't actively quit something — you just… stop doing it. It fades away because other things took over.

"His morning exercise habit fell by the wayside during the winter months."

4. Something fails to survive over time.
Businesses, trends, technologies, movements — things that once seemed important but quietly died out.

"Many social media platforms from the early 2000s have fallen by the wayside."
The Tone and Feeling of the Idiom

This idiom almost always carries a slightly sad or regretful tone. There is an unspoken sense of lost potential — whatever fell by the wayside had a chance, but didn't make it.

It is not a dramatic, explosive kind of failure. It's quieter than that. It suggests something that faded, drifted away, or was left behind — not something that blew up spectacularly.

Think of it as the difference between a candle that burns out versus one that gets knocked over and causes a fire. Falling by the wayside is the candle burning out.

Almost anything that involves effort, continuity, or progress over time:

  • Goals and ambitions → "His dream of writing a novel fell by the wayside."
  • Habits and routines → "Her diet fell by the wayside during the holidays."
  • Relationships → "Old friendships often fall by the wayside when people move to different cities."
  • Projects and plans → "The renovation project fell by the wayside due to a lack of funding."
  • People in a competition → "Half the contestants fell by the wayside in the first round."
  • Ideas and trends → "That technology fell by the wayside once smartphones took over."

It doesn't always mean someone is to blame.
Sometimes things fall by the wayside because of circumstances, bad timing, or external pressure — not personal failure. The idiom is neutral enough to cover both situations.

"The charity project fell by the wayside after the main organizer moved abroad." ← No blame, just circumstances.

"He let his health fall by the wayside because he cared too much about work." ← Here, there is a sense of personal neglect.

It implies something that once had momentum.
You can only fall by the wayside if you were on the path in the first place. This idiom always implies a starting point — an attempt, a beginning, a period of trying. You wouldn't use it for something that never started at all.

It is most natural in the past tense, but works in present and future too:

  • "fell by the wayside" (past — most common)
  • "has fallen by the wayside" (present perfect — still common)
  • "might fall by the wayside" (future possibility)
How It's Different From Similar Phrases

• "Give up" — more deliberate and personal. You decide to quit. Falling by the wayside is often more gradual and passive.
  • "Fail" — more direct and final. Falling by the wayside has a softer, more melancholy tone.
  • "Drop out" — similar, but usually about people leaving institutions (school, races). "Fall by the wayside" applies more broadly to ideas, habits, and plans too.
  • "Go by the wayside" — this is simply an alternate version of the same idiom. It means exactly the same thing.
One-Line Summary to Remember It Forever

"Fall by the wayside" = to start something but not make it to the end — whether because of failure, neglect, elimination, or simply being left behind.

Picture that seed on the hard ground beside the road. It had every chance. But it never grew. That's the heart of this idiom.
5942:
"Fall foul of" means to get into trouble with someone or something — especially by breaking a rule, violating a law, or doing something that causes conflict with a person or an authority.

Think of it this way: you were going along just fine, and then — suddenly — you clash with something or someone, and now you are in a bad situation because of it.
Breaking It Down

The word "foul" here does not mean a bad smell. In this idiom, "foul" means tangled, blocked, or in conflict with. This is an older use of the word that you won't see much in everyday speech anymore — it survives mainly inside this idiom.

So when you "fall foul of" something, you have essentially gotten tangled up with it in a harmful way.
Where Did It Come From?

This idiom has its roots in sailing and the sea. In old nautical (seafaring) language, when a ship's ropes, anchor, or chains became tangled or snagged on something — like rocks, another ship, or underwater obstacles — sailors would say the ship had "fallen foul of" that thing.

Over time, people started using it beyond sailing to describe any situation where someone gets caught up in trouble — with a law, a rule, a person, or an institution. Today, the nautical origin is completely forgotten in everyday use, but the meaning of "getting entangled in trouble" carried forward perfectly.
The Core Formula

Fall foul of + [a person / a rule / a law / an institution]

You always use this idiom with an object — meaning, you must say what or who someone has fallen foul of.
Detailed Examples With Explanations

1. Falling foul of the law / rules / regulations

"The company fell foul of environmental regulations and was heavily fined."

Here, the company broke environmental rules — probably without planning to — and faced serious consequences. They got into trouble with the law.

"He fell foul of tax rules by not declaring all his income."

He violated tax laws (whether intentionally or carelessly), and now he is in trouble with the authorities.

2. Falling foul of a person or group

"She fell foul of her manager after speaking out against the company's policy."

She said something that upset or angered her manager, creating conflict. Their relationship soured. She is now on bad terms with her boss.

"The journalist fell foul of powerful politicians who didn't like what he wrote."

The journalist's work angered those politicians, putting him in a dangerous or difficult situation with them.

3. Falling foul of a system or authority

"The young athlete fell foul of the anti-doping agency after a routine test."

The athlete got into trouble with the anti-doping organisation, possibly due to a failed drug test.
Important Nuance: Intentional or Accidental?

This is something many learners miss.

"Fall foul of" leans slightly toward accidents or carelessness — it often suggests that someone stumbled into trouble, perhaps not fully aware of the rules, or through a mistake. The word "fall" carries a sense of something happening to you, rather than a fully deliberate act.

However, it can also describe intentional wrongdoing — especially in news writing and journalism. So don't think it only means accidental trouble. The key point is simply that the person ended up in conflict with something or someone — and it caused them harm or difficulty.
Tense Changes — How to Use It in Different Times

The verb changes like any normal verb. Here are all the forms you need:

  • Present: "She often falls foul of the strict rules there."
  • Past (most common): "He fell foul of the law last year."
  • Past participle: "They have fallen foul of regulations before."
  • Present participle: "Falling foul of your superiors is never a good idea."
Register — When and Where Is It Used?

"Fall foul of" is slightly formal. You will see it very often in:

  • Newspapers and news articles (e.g., "The minister fell foul of his own party's rules.")
  • Legal or official writing
  • Books and literature

It is much more common in British English than American English. Americans tend to use the similar phrase "run afoul of" — which means exactly the same thing.

In casual spoken conversation, a native speaker might more simply say "got into trouble with" — but "fall foul of" is perfectly natural and sounds educated and precise, especially in writing.
Similar Expressions (For Extra Context)

Knowing these will help you understand the idiom even better by comparison:

  • "Run afoul of" — the American English equivalent. Identical in meaning.
  • "Get on the wrong side of" — to make someone dislike you or oppose you. (e.g., "Don't get on the wrong side of her.")
  • "Cross swords with" — to argue or clash with someone. (This focuses more on personal conflict.)
  • "Run into trouble with" — a more casual, everyday way of saying the same thing.

The difference is that "fall foul of" sounds more formal and is often used with institutions, laws, and rules — not just people.
A Quick Memory Trick

Picture a ship at sea. Its ropes get tangled in rocks near the shore. The ship is stuck. It's in trouble. It "fell foul of" the rocks.

Now replace the ship with a person, and replace the rocks with a rule, law, or authority figure.

The person got tangled up. The person is in trouble. The person fell foul of something.
Summary in One Sentence

"Fall foul of" means to get into trouble or conflict with a rule, law, authority, or person — often by accidentally or carelessly breaking something, or by doing something that causes someone powerful to turn against you.
5943:
To "fall from grace" means to lose the respect, favour, power, or good reputation that you once had — especially after doing something wrong, making a serious mistake, or behaving in a way that disappoints others.

Think of it this way: imagine someone standing on a high platform. Everyone below looks up at them with admiration and trust. Then, that person does something that shocks or disappoints everyone. Suddenly, they are knocked off that platform and fall down. That fall is what this idiom is talking about — not a physical fall, but a fall in people's eyes.

The "grace" in this idiom refers to a state of being highly regarded, trusted, or favoured — a kind of social, moral, or professional standing that people hold you in.
Where It Came From (The Origin)

This idiom has a deeply rooted religious origin, specifically from the Bible and Christian theology.

In the Bible, Adam and Eve lived in the Garden of Eden, where they enjoyed God's love and favour — they were in a state of grace (God's blessing and goodwill). But when they disobeyed God by eating the forbidden fruit, they lost that blessed state. They were cast out of Eden. This is called "The Fall" in Christian tradition — the moment humanity lost God's grace.

Over centuries, the phrase moved from its religious context into everyday language. Today, you do not need a religious setting at all to use it. It simply means anyone who had a high, respected position and then lost it through their own wrongdoing or failure.
Breaking Down the Words

To understand it fully, let's look at each word:

  • Fall — This doesn't mean a physical fall. It means a decline, a drop, a loss of something good.
  • From — It means away from, indicating movement out of a good place.
  • Grace — In everyday modern use, grace here means favour, respect, good standing, trust, or high reputation. It's the special status people gave you.

So together: moving away from a position of favour and respect.
How and When People Use It

This idiom is used when someone who was once admired, trusted, powerful, or respected has lost all of that — usually because of a scandal, a moral failure, dishonesty, or a serious mistake.

It is used in many different areas of life:

In politics:
A politician who was once loved by the public but was caught in a corruption scandal has "fallen from grace." The voters who once cheered for them now distrust or reject them.

In sports:
A champion athlete who was celebrated by millions but later got caught using performance-enhancing drugs has "fallen from grace." Their medals, their fame, and their heroic image all crumble.

In business:
A respected CEO who built a great company but was later found to have committed fraud has "fallen from grace." Colleagues, investors, and the public who once admired them now view them with disgust.

In personal life:
Even in smaller, everyday situations — a student who was a teacher's favourite but got caught cheating on an exam has "fallen from grace" in that teacher's eyes.
The Key Ingredients — What Must Be True for This Idiom to Apply

For this idiom to fit correctly, three things must be present:

  1. There was once a high status. The person must have been admired, trusted, powerful, or favoured before. You cannot fall from grace if you never had it in the first place.
  2. Something went wrong — usually through their own actions. The fall typically happens because of what the person themselves did — a mistake, wrongdoing, betrayal, or moral failure. It is rarely about bad luck alone.
  3. The loss is significant. It's not a minor setback. The respect, power, or reputation they lose is meaningful and substantial.
The Emotional Weight of the Idiom

This is an idiom that carries a sense of tragedy and disappointment. When you say someone has "fallen from grace," there is often an underlying feeling that:

  • They used to be good, or at least seemed good.
  • People believed in them.
  • The fall is sad, dramatic, and often public.

It's different from simply saying someone is "bad." It implies a contrast — they were once high up, and now they are not.
Grammar — How to Use It Correctly

The idiom works as a verb phrase. Here is how it changes with tense:

  • Present: "He is falling from grace."
  • Past: "She fell from grace after the scandal."
  • Perfect: "He has fallen from grace."
  • Infinitive: "She is about to fall from grace."

You can also use it as a noun phrase — "his fall from grace" or "her spectacular fall from grace." In this form, you're treating the whole event as a thing (a noun), not an action.

For example:
"The documentary explored the politician's fall from grace."
Variations and Related Expressions

These are phrases with very similar meanings that you may hear alongside this idiom:

  • "Out of favour" — simply means someone is no longer liked or trusted by someone important. It is less dramatic than "fall from grace."
  • "In disgrace" — means someone is currently in a state of shame or dishonour. Very similar in meaning.
  • "Lose one's reputation" — straightforward and literal, less poetic than "fall from grace."
  • "Downfall" — the noun describing the event when someone powerful loses everything.
  • "Rise and fall" — often used to describe someone's entire journey: their climb to power and their eventual ruin.
Real-World Example Sentences

Here are clear example sentences showing the idiom in natural use:

  • "The once-beloved actor fell from grace after multiple accusations of dishonesty came to light."
  • "Her fall from grace was painful to watch — just a year ago, she was the most admired person in the company."
  • "The corrupt minister's fall from grace shocked the entire nation."
  • "He was the golden boy of the team, but after the match-fixing scandal, he fell from grace almost overnight."
  • "Even great empires can fall from grace if their leaders become corrupt."
One Common Mistake to Avoid

Do not use this idiom for someone who simply fails at something or has bad luck. If a student studies hard but fails an exam, they haven't "fallen from grace" — they haven't lost anyone's respect through wrongdoing.

The idiom almost always suggests that the person's own behaviour caused their downfall. There is a moral or ethical dimension to it, which is what makes it feel weighty and serious.
The One-Line Summary

"Fall from grace" = to go from being highly respected, trusted, or favoured to being disgraced, rejected, or dishonoured — usually because of your own actions.

Once you know this idiom, you will start noticing it everywhere — in news articles, books, films, and everyday conversations. It is one of the English language's most powerful ways to describe the tragic collapse of someone's reputation or standing.
5944:
A fall guy is a person who ends up taking the blame or suffering the consequences for something — often for something that was not entirely (or not at all) their fault. Someone else — usually a more powerful or cleverer person — escapes punishment, while the fall guy is left to "fall" (face the music, take the hit, get in trouble).

The word has two closely related meanings. Both involve someone being put in an unfair position, but the situations are slightly different.

This is the primary and most widely used meaning.

A fall guy is a person who is deliberately set up or chosen to take the blame for someone else's wrongdoing. The real wrongdoer plans it this way — they engineer the situation so that when things go wrong, the fall guy gets punished instead of them.

The fall guy may be:

  • Completely innocent and falsely blamed.
  • Partially involved, but made to carry all the blame while the bigger fish swim free.

Key Features of this Meaning:

  • There is usually a deliberate, calculated act by someone to use the fall guy.
  • The fall guy is often someone with less power, less status, or less ability to defend themselves.
  • The person who escapes is usually the real mastermind — or at least more responsible.

Examples:

  • A corrupt politician commits fraud. His assistant, who only signed one document on his boss's orders, is arrested and prosecuted. The politician walks free. The assistant is the fall guy.
  • A gang robs a bank. The leader is careful to leave behind one inexperienced member to get caught, while the rest escape with the money. That left-behind member is the fall guy.
  • A company dumps toxic waste illegally. The CEO blames a low-level manager and fires him publicly to make it look like the company has taken action. The manager is the fall guy.

In all these cases, notice the pattern: someone more powerful uses someone less powerful as a human shield against consequences.
Meaning 2: An Easy Victim or a Sucker

In its second meaning, a fall guy refers to a person who is easily tricked, deceived, or taken advantage of — someone naïve or gullible enough that others can manipulate them without much effort.

Here, the emphasis is not necessarily on blame, but on vulnerability to manipulation. The fall guy in this sense is someone others look at and think, "That person is easy to fool."

Examples:

  • Con artists target a kind, trusting man and trick him into handing over his savings. He was their fall guy — someone they identified as easy to manipulate.
  • In a rigged card game, the professionals invite an overconfident amateur. They know he'll fall for every trick. He's the fall guy.

Both meanings share a common thread: the fall guy is on the losing end of someone else's scheme.

MeaningWhat happens to the fall guy
ScapegoatTakes the blame for others
Easy victimTakes the loss because of others

In real life, these meanings often overlap. A person who is set up as a scapegoat is usually chosen because they are easy to manipulate or lack the power to fight back.

• Fall guy is an informal, colloquial expression. You'll hear it in everyday conversation, news reporting, crime dramas, political discussions, and journalism.
  • It has a slightly cynical tone — using it implies that something unfair has happened or is being planned.
  • It is used almost always critically — to point out injustice, deception, or exploitation.
What a Fall Guy Is NOT

Understanding what something isn't is just as important:

  • A fall guy is not simply someone who made a mistake and faces consequences. If you genuinely caused a problem and face punishment for it, you are not a fall guy — you're just accountable.
  • A fall guy is not a volunteer martyr. A martyr chooses to suffer for a cause they believe in. A fall guy is usually pushed into that position — often without fully realizing it.
  • A fall guy is not necessarily a victim of random bad luck. There is almost always an element of someone using the fall guy on purpose.

A fall guy is someone who:

  1. Takes the blame or punishment that rightly (or more fully) belongs to someone else — often because they were deliberately set up that way (scapegoat meaning).
  2. Gets tricked or used by others because they are seen as an easy target (easy victim meaning).

The word captures a situation of unfairness, exploitation, and someone escaping responsibility at another person's expense. It is almost always used to describe something negative, unjust, or dishonest going on beneath the surface.
5945:
When something "falls on deaf ears," it means that a request, warning, advice, or plea was completely ignored — as if the listener simply did not hear it at all.

The person did hear the words physically, but they chose not to pay attention, not to care, or not to act on them. The message went in one ear and out the other, or perhaps never even registered at all.

In one line: Your words were heard, but nobody listened.
Breaking Down the Phrase

To understand this idiom deeply, look at its two parts:

  • "Deaf ears" — A deaf person cannot hear. So "deaf ears" refers to ears that are unable (or, in this case, unwilling) to receive a message.
  • "Fall on" — Imagine your words are like objects gently dropping down. They "fall on" the ears of the listener. If those ears are "deaf," the words simply land and vanish, making no impact.

So the full image is: your words dropped onto ears that could not — or would not — receive them.
The Key Idea: Ignored, Not Unspoken

This is very important. The idiom is not about failing to say something. It is about saying something and having it make no difference.

  • A parent who warns their teenager about staying out late — and the teenager ignores it completely — the warning fell on deaf ears.
  • A doctor who advises a patient to quit smoking, and the patient continues to smoke — the advice fell on deaf ears.
  • An employee who suggests a better strategy to their boss, and the boss dismisses it without consideration — the suggestion fell on deaf ears.

In every case, the message was delivered. The failure happened at the receiving end.
Feeling and Tone (Connotation)

This idiom carries a feeling of frustration, disappointment, or helplessness. When you say something fell on deaf ears, you are expressing that:

  • You tried to communicate something important.
  • The other person did not care.
  • Your effort felt wasted.

It is never a neutral phrase. There is always a sense that something should have been done differently by the listener.
Grammar: How to Use It Correctly

The structure of the idiom is:

[Something] fell / falls / has fallen on deaf ears.

The subject is always the message, advice, warning, request, or plea — not the person speaking.

✅ Correct:

  • "Her warnings fell on deaf ears."
  • "My suggestion seems to be falling on deaf ears."
  • "All our complaints have fallen on deaf ears."

❌ Incorrect:

  • "She fell on deaf ears." (A person cannot fall on deaf ears — only their words/message can.)

You can use it in past, present, or present perfect tense depending on when the ignoring happened.
Real-Life Example Sentences

Here are several examples across different situations so you can see exactly how the idiom is used naturally:

  1. At school: "The teacher repeatedly asked students to submit their assignments on time, but her requests fell on deaf ears."
  2. In a family: "My father warned my brother about his reckless spending, but as usual, his advice fell on deaf ears."
  3. At work: "The team raised concerns about the project's deadline being unrealistic, but their concerns fell on deaf ears."
  4. In politics: "The activists pleaded with the government to take action on pollution, but their pleas fell on deaf ears."
  5. In friendship: "I told her the relationship was not good for her, but my words fell on deaf ears — she went back to him anyway."

Notice how in every sentence, the speaker tried — but the listener simply did not act on it.
When Can You Use It?

You can use this idiom in both spoken English and written English. It works well in:

  • Everyday conversations
  • Essays and articles
  • News reporting
  • Speeches
  • Storytelling and literature

It is slightly formal to neutral in tone, so it fits comfortably in most situations — from a casual chat with a friend to a professional email or a news report.
Origin: Where Did This Idiom Come From?

The idiom is rooted in a very old and simple human experience — the feeling of not being listened to. The concept has existed in many languages and cultures for centuries.

The phrase in English goes back at least to the 16th century. One of its earliest known appearances is in the Bible (in various translations), where prophets or messengers speak to people who refuse to hear the truth. The idea of "deaf ears" as a symbol of willful ignorance is ancient.

Over time, the phrase became a fixed expression in everyday English to describe any situation where communication fails because the listener refuses to engage.
Similar Idioms (So You Can Compare)

Understanding related idioms helps you grasp the exact flavor of this one:

  • "Turn a deaf ear (to something)" — Very similar. It means to deliberately choose not to listen. "She turned a deaf ear to all his apologies." (Here, the focus is on the listener's active choice to ignore.)
  • "In one ear and out the other" — Means something was heard but immediately forgotten or ignored. It implies the listener is careless or forgetful.
  • "Talking to a wall" — Means speaking to someone who is completely unresponsive, as if they were a wall.
  • "Preaching to the wind" — Your words disappear without effect, like shouting into the wind.

The difference with "fall on deaf ears" is that it specifically highlights the futility of the attempt — you spoke, you tried, but nothing came of it.
A Common Mistake to Avoid

Do not confuse this idiom with situations where someone simply did not hear you (because of noise, distance, or an actual hearing impairment). This idiom is specifically about willful or indifferent ignoring — the listener could have acted on your words but chose not to.

Using it to describe a literal hearing problem would be awkward and incorrect.
Quick Summary

QuestionAnswer

What does it mean? → A message, advice, or warning was completely ignored.

Who ignored it? → The listener — the person the message was directed at.

What feeling does it carry? → Frustration, disappointment, helplessness.

What is the subject of the sentence? → The words/message/advice/warning — not the person.

Is it formal or informal? → Neutral — usable in both casual and formal contexts.

The next time someone keeps warning a friend about something and the friend keeps ignoring it, you will know exactly what to say: "All those warnings just fell on deaf ears."
5946:
To truly understand this idiom, you need to go back about 2,000 years to ancient Rome and Greece.

In those times, soldiers and military leaders actually carried swords. When a warrior faced total defeat — when there was no escape, no hope, and capture by the enemy was certain — he sometimes chose to die by his own sword rather than suffer the humiliation of being taken prisoner, tortured, or publicly shamed. He would point the sword at himself and fall onto it. This was considered an act of honor, not weakness. It said: "I would rather destroy myself than surrender my dignity."

Famous historical figures did this literally. Brutus, after losing the Battle of Philippi against Mark Antony and Octavian in 42 BC, fell on his sword. King Saul in the Bible did the same after a lost battle. It was a real, dramatic, and very final act.

Now fast-forward to the present. Nobody uses a sword anymore, but the idea behind that act — voluntarily harming yourself (your reputation, your career, your position) to preserve honor or protect others — is very much alive. That idea became an idiom.

"To fall on one's sword" means to voluntarily accept blame, punishment, or serious personal consequences — such as resigning from a job, publicly admitting fault, or sacrificing your own position — usually to protect someone else, a group, or an organization, or simply because it is the honorable thing to do.

The most important word here is voluntarily. The person is not being pushed out or forced. They are choosing to step up and say, "This is on me. I'll take the hit."

Think of it as a modern act of self-sacrifice — not with a sword, but with your career, reputation, or pride.
Breaking It Down With a Simple Example

Imagine a team of five people working on a big project at a company. The project fails badly and the boss is furious. In reality, all five people made mistakes. But one team member — the senior one — stands up in the meeting and says:

"This was my responsibility. I made the key decisions. I'll resign."

That person just fell on their sword. They took the blame and the consequences entirely upon themselves, even though it wasn't all their fault. They did it to protect the team, or because they genuinely felt responsible as the leader, or to end the crisis quickly.
The Core Ingredients of This Idiom

For someone to truly "fall on their sword," a few things are usually present:

1. A voluntary choice.
Nobody forced them. They chose to accept blame or step down on their own. This is what separates "falling on your sword" from simply "getting fired" or "being blamed." Being fired is something that happens to you. Falling on your sword is something you do.

2. A personal cost.
There must be a real sacrifice — a resignation, a public apology, damage to your reputation, loss of a position, or some form of serious consequence. It is not a small or casual thing.

3. A purpose beyond yourself.
The person usually does it for a reason bigger than themselves — to protect colleagues, to save an organization from further scandal, to restore public trust, or to uphold a sense of personal integrity and honor.
Where You'll Commonly Hear This Idiom

This idiom appears most often in formal and semi-formal contexts — politics, business, the military, and journalism. Here are the real-world situations where people use it:

In Politics:
A government minister resigns after a policy disaster, taking full public blame — even if the entire government was at fault — so that the Prime Minister or President is protected. News articles will say: "The minister fell on his sword to shield the administration."

In Business:
A CEO steps down after a company scandal and publicly accepts responsibility, even though the board of directors also played a role. This protects the company's reputation and signals accountability to shareholders.

In the Military:
An officer takes full responsibility for a failed mission and requests to be disciplined, even though multiple commanders were involved, because their personal code of honor demands it.

In Everyday Life:
A friend covers for another friend by saying "It was my idea, not theirs" to avoid getting the other person in trouble. That is a smaller, casual version of the same idea.
The Tone and Feeling of the Idiom

This idiom carries a generally respectful and sometimes admiring tone. When someone "falls on their sword," people often view them as honorable, responsible, or courageous — even if they also see it as unfortunate.

However, context matters. Sometimes the phrase is used with a hint of irony or cynicism, especially in politics, where someone is seen as "falling on their sword" only because they had no real choice — perhaps they were quietly pressured to resign — but it is being framed as a noble, voluntary act. In those cases, the idiom is used with a slightly skeptical eye.

So the emotional range goes from genuine admiration ("He fell on his sword — what a man of integrity") to mild sarcasm ("Oh sure, she 'fell on her sword' — they basically pushed her.")

Learners sometimes confuse this idiom with other expressions, so let's clear that up:

  • It does not mean to fail or make a mistake. The failure or crisis is what triggers the situation, but "falling on your sword" is the response to it — the act of stepping up and accepting consequences.
  • It does not mean to be punished by someone else. It is always a self-directed act.
  • It does not mean to give up or be a coward. Quite the opposite — it implies bravery and a sense of duty.
  • It is not the same as apologizing. An apology can be quick and painless. Falling on your sword involves real, significant sacrifice.

Here are some sentences to see the idiom in action, from simple to more advanced:

  • "Nobody expected him to fall on his sword, but he resigned the next morning and took all the blame."
  • "She fell on her sword to protect her team, even though the mistake wasn't entirely hers."
  • "The senator fell on his sword after the scandal, hoping it would save his party before the election."
  • "In that company, the culture expects senior managers to fall on their sword when projects fail — it's seen as leadership, not punishment."
One-Line Summary to Remember It Forever

"Fall on one's sword" = to voluntarily sacrifice your own position, reputation, or career by accepting blame or stepping down — usually to protect others or to act with honor.

The beauty of this idiom is that it has traveled 2,000 years from a literal battlefield to modern boardrooms and parliaments, and its soul has stayed exactly the same: the idea that sometimes, the most powerful thing a person can do is choose to bear the consequences themselves.
5947:
"Fall out with" is a phrasal verb. It means to have a disagreement or quarrel with someone that damages or strains your relationship with them.

The key idea hidden inside this phrase is that the argument doesn't just stay as a simple disagreement — it changes how two people feel about each other. Something breaks, or at least cracks, between them.

Think of it this way: imagine two people standing together on a bridge. They have a fight. Afterward, they are no longer standing together — they have fallen apart from each other. That is the emotional picture behind "fall out with."

"Fall out with" is made of three parts:

  • Fall — suggests something dropping, slipping, or moving away from where it was
  • Out — suggests a separation, a breaking away
  • With — connects the action to the other person involved

Together, they paint the picture of a relationship slipping out of its good, stable position because of a conflict.
What Makes This Phrase Special (Its Nuances)

Understanding the nuances is what separates a learner who knows a phrase from one who understands it deeply.

1. A relationship had to exist first.
You can only "fall out with" someone you were already connected to — a friend, a family member, a colleague, a neighbor. You cannot "fall out with" a total stranger because there was no relationship to damage in the first place.

Correct: "She fell out with her best friend."
Doesn't make sense: "She fell out with a random person she'd never met."

2. The disagreement harms the relationship.
This is the most important nuance. "Fall out with" is stronger than simply arguing. When you argue with someone, you might shake hands afterward and everything is fine. But when you "fall out with" someone, the argument leaves a mark. The two people become cold, distant, or even stop speaking altogether.

3. It can be temporary or permanent.
Sometimes people "fall out" and then make up a week later. Other times, they never speak again. The phrase itself doesn't tell you which — context does. This is important: "fall out with" covers both short-term and long-term rifts.

4. It is mostly informal.
This phrase is very natural in everyday speech and informal writing. It is not typically used in formal documents or academic writing. In formal contexts, you'd more likely see words like "dispute," "conflict," or "disagreement."

5. It is more common in British English.
If you read British novels, watch British TV, or speak with British people, you will hear this phrase constantly. It is also fully understood in American English, but Americans tend to use expressions like "have a falling-out with" or "got into it with" more often in casual speech.

See how the phrase works across different situations:

Example 1 — Friends:
"Tom fell out with his best friend over a misunderstanding about money."
→ They had an argument about money, and it damaged their friendship.

Example 2 — Family:
"She fell out with her sister years ago and they barely speak now."
→ A family quarrel long ago left a lasting distance between them.

Example 3 — Colleagues:
"He fell out with his manager after being overlooked for a promotion."
→ A work conflict created tension in their professional relationship.

Example 4 — Mutual falling out:
"The two business partners fell out with each other over the direction of the company."
→ Both sides share the conflict — no one person is entirely the "cause."

Example 5 — Recent and possibly temporary:
"I've fallen out with my flatmate, but I think we'll sort it out."
→ The quarrel is recent, and the speaker hopes it will be resolved.
All the Verb Forms You Need

Since "fall out with" is a phrasal verb, you need to know how to use it in different tenses.

  • Simple Present: "We fall out with each other sometimes, but we always make up."
  • Present Continuous: "They are falling out with each other right now over that decision."
  • Simple Past: "She fell out with him last year." (Note: the past tense of "fall" is "fell")
  • Present Perfect: "I have fallen out with my cousin, and I don't know how to fix it."
  • Past Perfect: "By the time I arrived, they had already fallen out with each other."
  • Infinitive: "I don't want to fall out with you over something so small."

The most commonly used tenses in real life are the simple past ("fell out with") and the present perfect ("have fallen out with"), because people usually talk about falling-outs after they have already happened.

The phrase has a noun form: "a falling-out." It means the same thing — a quarrel that damages a relationship — but used as a noun.

"We had a falling-out last summer, but we've since made up."
"Their falling-out over the inheritance tore the family apart."

This noun form is very useful and very natural. You will see it often.
How "Fall Out With" Differs from Similar Phrases

These phrases seem similar, but they are not identical:

"Argue with"
You can argue with someone and still be perfectly good friends afterward. Arguing is just disagreeing verbally. "Fall out with" implies that the relationship suffers as a result. All "falling-outs" involve arguing, but not all arguments lead to "falling out."

"Break up with"
This is only for romantic relationships. You break up with a girlfriend, boyfriend, or partner. "Fall out with" is for any kind of relationship — friends, family, colleagues.

"Lose touch with"
This means you stopped communicating over time — but not necessarily because of a fight. Maybe you both just got busy and drifted apart. "Fall out with" always involves a conflict, whereas "losing touch" may not involve any conflict at all.

"Clash with"
This means to have a conflict of opinions or personalities, often repeatedly. It focuses on the clash itself. "Fall out with" focuses more on the damage to the relationship that results from the clash.

ConceptThe Answer

"Fall out with" means to quarrel with someone in a way that hurts your relationship with them. It requires that a relationship existed first. The disagreement causes emotional distance, coldness, or a break in the relationship — either for a short time or permanently. It is an informal, everyday phrase, more common in British English. Its noun form is "a falling-out." It is stronger than simply "arguing" because it implies the relationship is damaged, not just the mood of the moment.

A natural way to remember this phrase is to associate it with the word "fallout" — as in the fallout from a disaster. When a disaster happens, the consequences spread far and wide. Similarly, when you "fall out with" someone, the fallout from that argument spreads into your relationship, leaving damage behind. Same root idea, same emotional weight.
5948:
"Fall short of" means to fail to reach a goal, standard, amount, or expectation — to come close, but not close enough.

Think of it this way: imagine you throw a ball trying to hit a target on a wall. The ball travels through the air but drops to the ground before reaching the wall. The ball fell short of the target. That physical image is the heartbeat of this phrase.

In everyday life, the "target" is rarely a physical thing. It is usually an expectation, a goal, a requirement, or a standard. And "falling short" means the result was less than what was needed or hoped for.

Understanding each word individually makes the whole phrase crystal clear.

Fall — Here, "fall" does not mean to trip or tumble. It means to land, to end up, or to come to rest at a certain point. Think of how rain "falls" or how night "falls." It is about arriving at a place or position.

Short — "Short" here means not enough, insufficient, or less than required. It is the same "short" as in "We are short on time" or "I'm a little short on cash" — meaning there isn't quite enough.

Of — This little word simply connects the phrase to what the target or standard is. "Of" points to the goal being missed.

So put together: something ended up (fell) at a point that was not enough (short) to reach a particular goal (of + the goal).

This is important: "fall short of" carries a gentle but clear sense of disappointment or inadequacy. It is not as harsh as saying "completely failed." Instead, it suggests that there was an effort or an expectation, and the result came close — but didn't quite make it.

It is also worth noting that "falling short" does not require blame. It is neutral in that sense. You can say a rainstorm fell short of forecasts — the rain didn't do anything wrong; it simply didn't meet the prediction.

Seeing a phrase in real-world situations is the best way to truly absorb it.

In business:
"The company's sales fell short of the target set at the beginning of the year."
(The sales were lower than the target.)

In sports:
"Despite playing brilliantly, the team fell short of winning the championship."
(They did not win, even though they played well.)

In personal life:
"His apology fell short of what she expected."
(The apology was not good enough to satisfy her.)

In academics:
"The essay fell short of the required word count."
(The essay had fewer words than required.)

In everyday speech:
"Our budget fell short of covering all the expenses."
(The money was not enough.)

Notice that in every example, there is always a gap — a space between what was and what was needed or expected.
Grammar: How to Use It Correctly

"Fall short of" is a phrasal verb. Here is the pattern:

Subject + fall short + of + noun (the goal/standard)

The verb "fall" changes its form depending on tense, just like any regular verb. Here are the most common forms:

Present: "The results fall short of expectations."
Past: "The results fell short of expectations."
Present Perfect: "The results have fallen short of expectations."
Future: "The results will fall short of expectations."

You can also drop the word "of" and simply say "fall short" when the target is already understood from the context.

"He tried his best, but he fell short."
(We understand he fell short of the goal already mentioned.)

English has several expressions that mean something very similar. Knowing them will help you understand "fall short of" even more deeply by comparison.

"Come up short" — Almost identical in meaning. "She came up short in the final round." (She didn't achieve the needed result.)

"Miss the mark" — To fail to hit the intended target or goal. "His presentation missed the mark."

"Not live up to" — To fail to meet expectations. "The film did not live up to the hype."

"Fail to meet" — More direct and formal. "The product failed to meet the quality standards."

All of these express the same central idea: a gap between what was expected and what actually happened.
The Opposite: When You Don't Fall Short

To fully own a phrase, you should also know what it contrasts with.

If you do not fall short, you either:

Meet expectations — you reached exactly what was needed.
"The project met all the requirements."

Exceed expectations — you went beyond what was needed, in a positive way.
"Her performance exceeded every expectation."

Live up to expectations — you fulfilled what was hoped for.
"The sequel lived up to the original film."

So the spectrum looks like this:

Fell short of → Met → Exceeded

"Fall short of" almost always implies there was a benchmark, standard, or expectation already set before the result happened. Without that pre-existing target, the phrase doesn't quite work.

For example, you wouldn't typically say, "He fell short of eating breakfast" — because eating breakfast isn't a standard or expectation that carries weight. But you would say, "He fell short of the fitness standards required for the job" — because there is a clear, defined benchmark.

The phrase lives in the space between trying and succeeding.

"Fall short of" means to fail to reach or achieve a required goal, standard, or expectation — to end up at a point that is less than what was needed or hoped for. It comes from the literal image of something (like an arrow or a throw) not traveling far enough to reach its target. It is used in formal and informal English, in business, sports, personal life, and beyond. It always implies there was a gap between the desired result and the actual result — and that gap is what "falling short" describes.
5949:
Before we get to how people actually use this phrase in everyday life, picture this:

You're walking across a wooden bridge. One of the planks is rotten. Your foot lands on it — and instead of standing firm, it breaks, and your leg falls through the hole. It goes down. It disappears into the gap. It never reaches a solid destination.

That physical image — something going downward, disappearing through a gap, never completing its journey — is the root of everything this phrase means.
The Core Meaning: The Idiomatic Use

In everyday English, "fall through" is a phrasal verb (a verb + a preposition that together create a new meaning). It is used figuratively — meaning it is rarely about anything physically falling.

It means: a plan, deal, arrangement, or agreement fails to happen or be completed.

When something "falls through," it was moving forward — it was being planned, negotiated, or arranged — but then it collapsed, broke down, and never reached its destination. Just like that leg falling through the rotten plank.

"The business deal fell through at the last minute."

The deal was being worked on. People were negotiating. It was heading somewhere. Then — it didn't happen. It disappeared into the gap. It fell through.
Key Things to Understand About This Meaning

1. Something has to have been "in motion" first.

You can't say a plan "fell through" if it was never really being pursued. The phrase implies the thing was actually underway — being planned, arranged, or expected — before it failed. There's a sense of process that didn't complete.

2. It carries disappointment.

When something falls through, it's almost always unwanted. There's an implied sense of loss, frustration, or surprise. You were expecting something, and it didn't come to be.

3. The failure often happens near the end.

"Fall through" often implies the failure happened after significant effort or progress — not right at the beginning. This is what makes it especially disappointing.

4. It's often nobody's "fault," or the fault is unspoken.

Unlike saying "he ruined the deal," saying "the deal fell through" is more neutral and passive — it simply states the outcome without necessarily blaming anyone. This is why it's used so often in professional and polite contexts.
Grammar: How to Use It Correctly

"Fall through" follows normal English verb conjugation:

  • Present: The plan falls through all the time in situations like this.
  • Past (most common): The plan fell through.
  • Present continuous: The deal is falling through as we speak.
  • Present perfect: The deal has fallen through.
  • Future: I'm worried the arrangement will fall through.

Notice something important: you don't put an object after "fall through." You don't say "the deal fell through them." The subject — the plan, the deal, the arrangement — is the thing that falls through. The phrase is intransitive, meaning it doesn't take a direct object.

✅ "The sale fell through."
❌ "They fell through the sale." (This sounds like they physically dropped through the sale, which makes no sense.)

Business and money:

  • "We were about to close the deal on the company merger, but it fell through when the lawyers couldn't agree on the terms."
  • "The investment fell through at the last second. The backer pulled out."
  • "My job offer fell through. The company had a hiring freeze."

Real estate (buying/selling homes):

  • "We found a perfect house, made an offer, and then the sale fell through because the inspection revealed serious damage."
  • "Three buyers have shown interest, but every deal falls through before closing."

Plans and events:

  • "We were going to throw a surprise party, but it fell through because half the guests canceled."
  • "My trip to Japan fell through — I lost my passport."
  • "The concert fell through when the main artist got injured."

Relationships and personal life:

  • "I had a date planned for Saturday, but it fell through."
  • "Our plans to move in together fell through after the relationship ended."

Projects and ideas:

  • "The documentary project fell through when they ran out of funding."
  • "We had a great idea for a startup, but it fell through in the planning stage."

"Fall through" vs. "Fall apart"

These sound similar and both suggest failure, but they mean different things.

  • Fall through = a specific plan, deal, or arrangement fails to happen.
  • Fall apart = something that already exists starts to break down or deteriorate. It can also describe broader things like a relationship, a system, or someone's composure.

"The deal fell through." — The deal never happened.
"The company fell apart after the CEO left." — The company existed but then deteriorated from within.

"Fall through" vs. "Fall out"

  • Fall through = a plan fails.
  • Fall out = people have a disagreement or argument, often ending a relationship or friendship.

"The project fell through." — The project didn't happen.
"They fell out over money." — They had a dispute and their relationship was damaged.

"Fall through" vs. "Not work out"

These are close in meaning, but "fall through" is more specific — it often implies the thing was further along before it failed, and it has a slightly more sudden or sharp feeling to it. "Not work out" is broader and softer.

"It didn't work out" — gentle, general, could mean it was a bad fit.
"It fell through" — sharper, more specific, implies it was underway and then collapsed.
The Phrase as a Noun Phrase

Sometimes people turn this into a noun by saying "a fall-through" (hyphenated). This is less common but you may hear it.

"We had a fall-through on the sale. We're back to square one."
One Special Use: In Programming (For Reference)

If you ever encounter this phrase in a computer science or coding context, it means something different. In programming languages like C, Java, or JavaScript, a "fall-through" refers to what happens inside a switch statement when one case doesn't have a break instruction — the code keeps running and "falls through" into the next case automatically, like water falling through to the next level.

"Watch out for the fall-through bug in that switch statement — you forgot to add a break."

This is a completely separate technical meaning, borrowed from the same physical image (something falling downward into the next space), but used only in programming discussions.

AspectDetails

"Fall through" is a phrasal verb. Its primary everyday meaning is that a plan, deal, arrangement, or agreement fails to be completed — it was in progress, it was expected, but it collapsed before reaching its destination. It carries a sense of disappointment and is often used in a neutral, slightly passive way to describe the failure without blaming anyone directly. It is intransitive (no object follows it). Its past tense is "fell through," which is by far the most common form you will encounter. It is different from "fall apart" (which describes deterioration of something existing) and "fall out" (which describes a dispute between people). In programming, it has a separate, technical meaning related to switch statement behavior.

If you remember just one thing: when a plan "falls through," it was going somewhere — and then it didn't. It dropped into the gap and disappeared, just like that leg through the rotten plank.
